title: Cell Biology & Genetics — DNA, Genes & Heredity

subChunks.title: Cell Biology & Genetics — DNA, Genes & Heredity

storyBeats.txt: In 1953, Theodora said, Watson and Crick published a two-page paper with the understatement of the century: 'It has not escaped our notice that the specific pairing we have postulated immediately suggests a possible copying mechanism for the genetic material.' That possible copying mechanism turned out to be the entire mechanism of heredity.

The double helix was not just a beautiful structure — it was a data storage device. Four bases, arranged along two complementary strands, encoding every protein your body will ever make, every feature you will ever have. The language of life is a four-letter alphabet.

And Mendel — working with peas decades before anyone knew what DNA was — had already worked out the inheritance rules that flow from it. The patterns of heredity emerged before their molecular mechanism was understood. That is often how science works.

subChunks.hookHtml: Genetics is the science of heredity — how biological information is stored, transmitted, and expressed. At its molecular core is DNA, the molecule that stores genetic information in every living cell. Understanding how DNA is structured, how it is copied and expressed as protein, and how it is inherited from parents to offspring gives you the foundation of modern biology, medicine, agriculture, and forensic science.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
DNA Structure

DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) is a double-stranded helix. Each strand is a polymer of nucleotides. A nucleotide consists of: a deoxyribose sugar + a phosphate group + one of four nitrogenous bases.

The four bases and their complementary pairs:

  • Adenine (A) pairs with Thymine (T) — two hydrogen bonds
  • Guanine (G) pairs with Cytosine (C) — three hydrogen bonds

The two strands run antiparallel (5'→3' and 3'→5'). The sequence of bases along a strand encodes genetic information. The human genome contains approximately 3.2 billion base pairs, packaged into 23 pairs of chromosomes in the nucleus.

DNA Replication

Before cell division, DNA is copied (replicated) so each daughter cell receives a complete genome. Key steps:

  1. Helicase unwinds and separates the double helix.
  2. DNA polymerase reads each strand (3'→5') and synthesises a new complementary strand (5'→3') by adding complementary nucleotides.
  3. Result: two identical double-stranded DNA molecules, each containing one original and one new strand (semi-conservative replication — confirmed by Meselson-Stahl experiment, 1958).

The Central Dogma: DNA → RNA → Protein

Genetic information flows in one direction (with some exceptions):

Transcription (DNA → RNA): In the nucleus, RNA polymerase reads the DNA template strand (3'→5') and synthesises a complementary messenger RNA (mRNA) strand (5'→3'). RNA uses uracil (U) instead of thymine (T). The mRNA carries the genetic message from the nucleus to the ribosome.

Translation (mRNA → Protein): At the ribosome, the mRNA sequence is read in triplets (codons). Each codon specifies one amino acid, decoded by transfer RNA (tRNA) molecules carrying the correct amino acid. The ribosome links amino acids together to form a polypeptide chain, which folds into a functional protein. The genetic code: 64 codons specify 20 amino acids (the code is redundant — multiple codons can specify the same amino acid). Three codons are 'stop' codons; one (AUG) is the 'start' codon encoding methionine.

Gene Expression and Regulation

Not all genes are expressed in all cells at all times. Gene expression is regulated by transcription factors, promoter sequences, and epigenetic modifications (DNA methylation, histone modification). A liver cell and a neuron contain identical DNA but express very different sets of genes — this differential gene expression is what makes cell differentiation possible.

Mutations

A mutation is any change in the DNA sequence. Types:

  • Point mutation: Single base changed (substitution), deleted, or inserted. A missense mutation changes one amino acid; a nonsense mutation creates a stop codon (truncating the protein); a silent mutation changes a codon but not the amino acid (due to degeneracy of the genetic code).
  • Frameshift mutation: Insertion or deletion of base(s) not in multiples of three — shifts the reading frame, typically garbling the protein sequence from that point.
  • Chromosomal mutation: Large-scale changes — deletion, duplication, inversion, or translocation of chromosomal segments.

Mutations are the raw material of evolution — most are neutral or harmful, but rare beneficial mutations provide variation for natural selection to act on. Mutagens include UV radiation, ionising radiation, and certain chemicals.

Mendelian Genetics

Gregor Mendel's experiments with garden peas (1866) established the principles of inheritance:

  • Law of Segregation: Each organism carries two alleles for each trait (one from each parent); these alleles separate during gamete formation. Each gamete carries one allele.
  • Law of Independent Assortment: Alleles for different traits assort independently into gametes (true for genes on different chromosomes).

Key terms: allele (variant of a gene); homozygous (two identical alleles); heterozygous (two different alleles); dominant (expressed in heterozygote); recessive (only expressed when homozygous); genotype (genetic makeup, e.g., Aa); phenotype (observable characteristic).

Punnett squares allow prediction of offspring genotype ratios. A cross between two heterozygotes (Aa × Aa) gives a 3:1 phenotype ratio (3 dominant : 1 recessive) and a 1:2:1 genotype ratio (AA : Aa : aa).

Sex-Linked Inheritance

Some genes are carried on sex chromosomes (X and Y). Genes on the X chromosome are X-linked. Males (XY) have only one copy of X-linked genes, so recessive X-linked traits (e.g., red-green colour blindness, haemophilia A) are expressed more frequently in males than females.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a 16-year-old how a four-letter code (A, T, G, C) can encode all the information needed to build a human being — and how that information gets translated into proteins.
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml: Two parents are both carriers of cystic fibrosis (CF). CF is an autosomal recessive condition. Carrier means the individual has one working copy (C) and one faulty copy (c) of the CFTR gene (genotype Cc). (1) Using a Punnett square, predict the probability that each child will: (a) have CF; (b) be a carrier; (c) be unaffected and not a carrier. (2) If these parents have four children, explain why it is not guaranteed that exactly one will have CF. (3) The CF mutation most common in Europe (deltaF508) is a deletion of three bases coding for phenylalanine at position 508. What type of mutation is this? (4) Explain why CF follows an autosomal recessive pattern rather than a dominant one.
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
(1) Punnett square: Cc × Cc:
C c
C | CC | Cc |
c | Cc | cc |
(a) Have CF (cc): 1/4 = 25%. (b) Carrier (Cc): 2/4 = 50%. (c) Unaffected non-carrier (CC): 1/4 = 25%.

(2) Each pregnancy is an independent event with a 25% chance of CF. Having four children does not guarantee one will have CF — it makes it probable (expected 1 in 4) but probability applies to large numbers of independent events, not individual outcomes. The parents could have zero, one, two, or more affected children — it is chance. (The binomial probability of exactly one out of four having CF is ≈42%; the probability of zero is ≈32%.)

(3) The deltaF508 mutation is a deletion of three bases (a trinucleotide deletion). Because three bases = one codon, this is an in-frame deletion — it removes one amino acid (phenylalanine at position 508) without causing a frameshift. The resulting protein is missing one amino acid and folds incorrectly.

(4) CF is recessive because one working copy of the CFTR gene produces enough functional CFTR chloride channel protein for normal cell function. Heterozygous individuals (Cc) have 50% of normal CFTR expression — sufficient to avoid disease. Only individuals with two non-functional alleles (cc) cannot make any functional CFTR and therefore develop CF. If CF were dominant, one faulty copy would be enough to cause disease, and carriers would be affected.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Sickle-cell disease is caused by a point mutation in the HBB gene encoding beta-haemoglobin: a single A→T substitution changes the sixth codon from GAG (glutamic acid) to GTG (valine). Sickle-cell trait (carrying one normal and one sickle allele) provides partial protection against malaria. (1) What type of mutation is this? (2) How does a single amino acid change cause red blood cells to deform into sickle shapes? (3) Use evolutionary reasoning to explain why sickle-cell disease remains common in malaria-endemic regions despite being a serious illness when homozygous. (4) Why would you predict that sickle-cell disease is more common in equatorial Africa and less common in northern Europe?
subChunks.modelAnswer:
(1) This is a point mutation — specifically a missense substitution: a single base change (A to T) that changes the amino acid at position 6 of beta-globin from glutamic acid to valine. It is not a nonsense mutation (does not create a stop codon), not a silent mutation (the amino acid changes), and not a frameshift (a single substitution, not an insertion or deletion).

(2) Glutamic acid (charged, hydrophilic) at position 6 is replaced by valine (uncharged, hydrophobic). This creates a hydrophobic patch on the surface of the haemoglobin molecule. When oxygen concentration is low, the hydrophobic patch causes haemoglobin molecules to polymerise into long fibres, distorting the red blood cell into a rigid sickle shape. Sickled cells: block capillaries (causing pain crises); have a shorter lifespan (haemolytic anaemia); are less deformable than normal round cells.

(3) This is a classic case of heterozygote advantage (balancing selection). Individuals with two sickle alleles (SS) have sickle-cell disease — severely disadvantaged, reduced survival and fertility. Individuals with two normal alleles (AA) are healthy but fully susceptible to malaria — in malaria-endemic regions, many die young. Individuals with one of each (AS — sickle-cell trait) have mild protection against severe malaria (the sickle allele disrupts the malaria parasite's lifecycle in red blood cells) AND do not have sickle-cell disease. Heterozygotes are the most reproductively fit in malarial environments — this maintains both alleles in the population at a stable intermediate frequency, a phenomenon called a balanced polymorphism. Neither allele is fully eliminated by natural selection.

(4) Malaria (Plasmodium falciparum) is transmitted by Anopheles mosquitoes, which thrive in warm, wet tropical climates. In equatorial Africa, malaria transmission is intense and year-round; the survival advantage of sickle-cell trait is significant. In northern Europe, malaria is absent (or historically very rare and mild); there is no survival advantage to carrying the sickle allele. In the absence of selection pressure from malaria, the sickle allele is only a disadvantage (when homozygous, causing disease). Over generations, natural selection has eliminated the sickle allele from northern European populations, while maintaining it at high frequency in sub-Saharan African populations.
learningObjectives: Describe the structure of DNA, including the four bases, base-pairing rules, and the antiparallel double-helix structure.
Outline the central dogma (DNA → RNA → protein) and explain the roles of transcription and translation.
Classify mutations (point, frameshift, chromosomal) and explain how each affects protein structure.
Apply Mendel's laws and Punnett squares to predict offspring genotype and phenotype ratios for monohybrid crosses.
commonMistakes: Confusing DNA replication with transcription — replication copies DNA to DNA before cell division; transcription copies DNA to RNA for protein synthesis.
Forgetting that RNA uses uracil (U) instead of thymine (T) — in transcription, A in the DNA template pairs with U in the mRNA.
Treating Mendelian ratios as guarantees — they are probabilities based on many offspring; individual families may not match the ratio.
Assuming dominant means more common — dominant alleles are expressed over recessive ones in heterozygotes, but have no necessary relationship to allele frequency in the population.
assessmentCriteria: Correctly describes base-pairing rules and explains what changes at each step of the central dogma.
Accurately classifies a described mutation and predicts its effect on the resulting protein.
Draws a correct Punnett square and calculates genotype/phenotype probabilities for a monohybrid cross.
Explains heterozygote advantage and balancing selection using sickle-cell disease as an example.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: DNA replication produces two daughter molecules each containing one original strand and one new strand — confirmed by Meselson and Stahl (1958) using nitrogen isotope labelling.
Francis Crick's 1958 formulation: genetic information flows from DNA to RNA to protein — not in reverse (with the exception of reverse transcriptase in retroviruses like HIV).
A sequence of three mRNA bases that specifies one amino acid during translation — 64 codons encode 20 amino acids (redundant code); three are stop codons; one (AUG) is the start codon.
The maintenance of two alleles in a population at stable frequencies because heterozygotes have higher fitness than either homozygote — sickle-cell and malaria is the classic example.

Heritable changes in gene expression that do not involve changes in DNA sequence — DNA methylation, histone modification, and chromatin remodelling control which genes are expressed in different cell types.

questions.questionHtml: During DNA transcription, which statement correctly describes what happens?
options: DNA polymerase copies both strands of DNA to produce two new double-stranded DNA molecules
RNA polymerase reads the template strand of DNA (3' to 5') and synthesises a complementary mRNA strand, using uracil instead of thymine
Ribosomes read the mRNA sequence and assemble amino acids into a polypeptide
Helicase unwinds the DNA helix and DNA polymerase adds complementary bases to each strand
questions.correctAnswer: RNA polymerase reads the template strand of DNA (3' to 5') and synthesises a complementary mRNA strand, using uracil instead of thymine
questions.explanationHtml: Transcription: RNA polymerase binds to the promoter sequence and reads the template (antisense) DNA strand in the 3'→5' direction, synthesising mRNA 5'→3'. RNA uses uracil (U) where DNA uses thymine (T) — otherwise the base-pairing rules are the same (A pairs with U; G pairs with C). The ribosome-tRNA process described in option 3 is translation, not transcription. Option 4 describes DNA replication.

questions.questionHtml: Two parents are both carriers of an autosomal recessive condition (Aa × Aa). What is the probability that their next child will be an unaffected carrier (Aa)?
questions.explanationHtml: Punnett square for Aa × Aa: possible offspring are AA (25%), Aa (50%), aa (25%). The probability of genotype Aa (carrier, unaffected) is 50%. Note: the question asks specifically for carriers (Aa), not all unaffected individuals — AA (25%) is also unaffected but not a carrier. Common error: confusing unaffected (75%) with carrier (50%).

questions.questionHtml: A mutation inserts a single extra base into the coding sequence of a gene, 20 base pairs before the end of the gene. What is the most likely consequence?
options: A single amino acid is changed near the end of the protein — the protein is mostly normal
The protein is completely normal — a single base insertion rarely has an effect
A frameshift occurs: the reading frame shifts from the insertion point, scrambling almost all codons from that point onward, producing a severely abnormal protein
The mutation creates a stop codon that terminates the protein 20 amino acids early
questions.correctAnswer: A frameshift occurs: the reading frame shifts from the insertion point, scrambling almost all codons from that point onward, producing a severely abnormal protein
questions.explanationHtml: A single-base insertion creates a frameshift mutation: every codon from the insertion point onward is read in a shifted register, producing a completely different — typically non-functional — amino acid sequence from that point. Since codons are read in non-overlapping triplets, adding one base disrupts all downstream codons. The mutation is 20 bp from the end, so the last ~7 amino acids (and likely a novel premature stop codon) will be scrambled. Even a single-base insertion near the end of a gene typically destroys protein function. Option 4 describes a nonsense (point) mutation, not a frameshift.
